name: Geiger–Marsden (1909)
description: Alpha particles fired at gold foil sometimes bounced straight back: the atom has a tiny, heavy, positive nucleus. Steer the alpha near the source so that it backscatters into the detector. The deflection follows $\tan(\theta/2) = qQ/(2T_0 b)$: the impact parameter b decides everything.

reality.represents: Rutherford scattering: alpha particles off a gold nucleus

remarks.detail: The deflection follows tan(θ/2) = qQ/(2T₀b). For the Coulomb force quantum mechanics gives the same scattering as classical mechanics, which is why Rutherford's classical analysis was right.

remarks.line: One alpha aimed at one nucleus
remarks.detail: Geiger and Marsden fired many alphas through a gold foil thousands of atoms thick; each met nuclei at random distances and about 1 in 8000 bounced back. Here you aim one alpha at one nucleus.
It is held fixed. A gold nucleus, 49 times heavier than an alpha, recoils a little: an alpha bouncing straight back loses about 8 % of its energy to it.
They screen the nucleus only far from it and are far too light to deflect the alpha; they are left out.
A 5 MeV alpha comes within about 45 fm of a gold nucleus head-on; the cell-sized board is the same physics scaled up (the Scales section).
